{{Short description|Matrix whose determinant is a resultant}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Bézout matrix''' (or '''Bézoutian''' or '''Bezoutiant''') is a special [[square matrix]] associated with two [[polynomial]]s, introduced by [[James Joseph Sylvester]] in 1853 and [[Arthur Cayley]] in 1857 and named after [[Étienne Bézout]].{{sfn|Sylvester|1853}}{{sfn|Cayley|1857}} 
'''Bézoutian''' may also refer to the [[determinant]] of this matrix, which is equal to the [[resultant]] of the two polynomials. Bézout matrices are sometimes used to test the [[stable polynomial|stability]] of a given polynomial.

==Definition==
Let <math>f(z)</math> and <math>g(z)</math> be two [[complex number|complex]] polynomials of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] at most ''n'',
:<math>f(z) = \sum_{i=0}^n u_i z^i,\qquad g(z) = \sum_{i=0}^n v_i z^i.</math>
(Note that any [[coefficient]] <math>u_i</math> or <math>v_i</math> could be zero.) The '''Bézout matrix''' of order ''n'' associated with the polynomials ''f'' and ''g'' is 
:<math>B_n(f,g)=\left(b_{ij}\right)_{i,j=0,\dots,n-1}</math>
where the entries <math>b_{ij}</math> result from the identity
:<math>
  \frac{f(x)g(y)-f(y)g(x)}{x-y}
     =\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1} b_{ij}\,x^{i}\,y^{j}.
</math>

It is an ''n'' × ''n'' complex matrix, and its entries are such that if we let <math>\ell_{ij} = \max\{0,i-j\}</math> and <math>m_{ij} = \min\{i,n-1-j\}</math> for each <math>i, j = 0, \dots, n-1</math>, then:
:<math>b_{ij}=\sum_{k=\ell_{ij}}^{m_{ij}}(u_{j+k+1}v_{i-k}-u_{i-k}v_{j+k+1}).</math>

To each Bézout matrix, one can associate the following [[bilinear form]], called the Bézoutian:
:<math>\operatorname{Bez}: \mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}: (x,y)\mapsto \operatorname{Bez}(x,y) = x^{*}B_n(f,g)\,y.</math>

==Examples==
* For ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3, we have for any polynomials ''f'' and ''g'' of degree (at most) 3:
::<math>B_3(f,g)=\left[\begin{matrix}u_1v_0-u_0 v_1 & u_2 v_0-u_0 v_2 & u_3 v_0-u_0 v_3\\u_2 v_0-u_0 v_2 & u_2v_1-u_1v_2+u_3v_0-u_0v_3 & u_3 v_1-u_1v_3\\u_3v_0-u_0v_3 & u_3v_1-u_1v_3 & u_3v_2-u_2v_3\end{matrix}\right]\!.</math>

* Let <math>f(x) = 3x^3-x</math> and <math>g(x) = 5x^2+1</math> be the two polynomials.  Then:
::<math>B_4(f,g)=\left[\begin{matrix}-1 & 0 & 3 & 0\\0 &8 &0 &0 \\3 & 0 & 15 & 0\\0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix}\right]\!.</math>
The last row and column are all zero as ''f'' and ''g'' have degree strictly less than ''n'' (which is 4).  The other zero entries are because for each <math>i = 0, \dots, n</math>, either <math>u_i</math> or <math>v_i</math> is zero.

==Properties==
* <math>B_n(f,g)</math> is [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] (as a matrix);
* <math>B_n(f,g) = -B_n(g,f)</math>;
* <math>B_n(f,f) = 0</math>;
* <math>(f, g) \mapsto B_n(f,g)</math> is a [[bilinear map|bilinear]] function;
* <math>B_n(f,g)</math> is a real matrix if ''f'' and ''g'' have [[real number|real]] coefficients;
* <math>B_n(f,g)</math> is nonsingular with <math>n=\max(\deg(f),\deg(g))</math> if and only if ''f'' and ''g'' have no common [[zero of a function|roots]].
* <math>B_n(f,g)</math> with <math>n = \max(\deg(f),\deg(g))</math> has [[determinant]] which is the [[resultant]] of ''f'' and ''g''.
* Bezoutians can be reduced to block diagonal form with the help of [[Vandermonde matrix#Confluent Vandermonde matrices|confluent Vandermonde matrix]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bini |first1=D.A. |last2=Mehrmann |first2=V. |last3=Olshevsky |first3=V. |date=2010 |title= Numerical Methods for Structured Matrices and Applications, Operator Theory: Advances and Applications Book 199 |at=Proposition 9.7  |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-3-7643-8996-3  |doi=10.1007/978-3-7643-8996-3 }}</ref>

==Applications==
An important application of Bézout matrices can be found in [[control theory]].  To see this, let ''f''(''z'') be a complex polynomial of degree ''n'' and denote by ''q'' and ''p'' the real polynomials such that ''f''(i''y'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''q''(''y'')&nbsp;+&nbsp;i''p''(''y'') (where ''y'' is real).  We also denote ''r'' for the [[rank of a matrix|rank]] and ''&sigma;'' for the signature of <math>B_n(p,q)</math>.  Then, we have the following statements:
* ''f''(''z'') has ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''r'' roots in common with its conjugate;
* the left ''r'' roots of ''f''(''z'') are located in such a way that:
** (''r''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''&sigma;'')/2 of them lie in the open left half-plane, and
** (''r''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''&sigma;'')/2 lie in the open right half-plane;
* ''f'' is [[stable polynomial|Hurwitz stable]] if and only if <math>B_n(p,q)</math> is [[Positive-definite matrix|positive definite]].

The third statement gives a necessary and sufficient condition concerning stability.  Besides, the first statement exhibits some similarities with a result concerning [[Sylvester matrix|Sylvester matrices]] while the second one can be related to [[Routh–Hurwitz theorem]].
